source_propositions.source_text: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.
An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire and causing injuries, according to Saudi authorities.
Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.
The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.
After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”

The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.
Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.
The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.
The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.
The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.

source_propositions.source_text: A drone attack by Sudan's paramilitary forces has killed 41 people in the country's Blue Nile region bordering Ethiopia, a rights group has said.
The strike by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted a camp for displaced people in the state's Abu Shandi area on Friday, Emergency Lawyers said.
The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said it was "appalled by horrifying reports". It said initial reports suggested most of the casualties were women and children.

The Sudanese army and paramilitary forces including the RSF have been locked in a power struggle since 2023, a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million from their homes. It has also created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with millions of people needing medical help.
The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south.
Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill.
Truckloads of Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving into Ethiopia, which has reportedly responded with drone strikes.
South Africa has experienced recurrent outbreaks of violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.

source_propositions.source_text: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on.

Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.

The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.
The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.

However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.
So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?
Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.

In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray.
The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger.
Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving.

source_propositions.source_text: Kyiv, Ukraine — At least 33 people were killed on Thursday when a Russian strike caused two public buses to catch fire in eastern Ukraine, local authorities said, making it the deadliest single attack this year.

Another 18 people were injured in the attack in Kramatorsk, a city in the Donetsk region, which prompted authorities there to shut down the public transport system and urge people to move to safer parts of the country.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” said Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration.
“For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.”
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) said the Russian strike caused a fire on two buses and in the surrounding area.
Police in Donetsk said Russian drones targeted officers who were helping victims of the strike.
Police were still working to identify the victims of the strike, with some bodies having to be pieced together from fragments, they said in a statement.
Drones can be seen near the scene of the strike as responders load the injured onto stretchers and into emergency vehicles.
One emergency worker can be heard asking an injured woman for her name.

“Russia is bringing death to Ukrainian soil. It is striking our cities, killing our people, and multiplying its crimes every day,” added Filashkin as he offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of victims.
A mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage.
In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv.

items.sourceTitle: Hurricane Isaias kills at least four, leaves thousands without power in US

source_propositions.source_text: A backyard is flooded in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Destin, Florida, US.
( Reuters: Marco Bello ) Hurricane Isaias has killed at least four people, leaving hundreds of thousands without power across three US states.
Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared emergencies.
Hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes were expected across parts of the US, the National Hurricane Center said.
At least four people have died and 800,000 Florida, Alabama and Georgia residents were without power after Hurricane Isaias made landfall.
Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said.
However, hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US were expected, the National Hurricane Center said.
( Reuters: Marco Bello ) In Florida, power restoration was marked as priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage.
"They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," Mr DeSantis said.
In Alabama and Florida, three people were killed by falling trees, according to local media and authorities.
"A tree fell on a house and unfortunately took the life of a lady," he said, and later confirmed that a man died from carbon monoxide poisoning.
Isaias rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season.

items.sourceTitle: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’

source_propositions.source_text: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy , who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social. He offered no further details.
Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same.
“If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”.
“It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.

items.sourceTitle: Pakistan imposes emergency rule over Imran Khan's provincial government

sources.title: 'President promulgates emergency, governor's rule in KP'
propositions: Minister for Law and Justice Senator Azam Nazeer Tarar has said the President, on the advice of the Prime Minister, today promulgated Emergency and Governor's Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution.

He was addressing a joint news conference in Islamabad this evening along with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister for Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry, and MNA Samar Bilour.
Azam Nazeer Tarar said under the Constitution, the provincial government led by the Chief Minister has ceased to exist.
He said all the powers that rested with the Chief Minister, the provincial cabinet, and the advisors have been handed over to the Governor.
The Minister for Law said an eleven-member Advisory Council has been constituted, which will work under the Governor to run the government's affairs.

He further said that under another proclamation, a separate Secretariat has been established under the Governor and the Chief Secretary to run affairs of twelve districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa which will be directly under the Federation.

The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in theprovince intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan's release.
The party’s last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces and Khan’s 2023 arrest sparked nationwide riots that threatened the military’s standing.
Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters have been detained ahead of the planned march, in what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years.

Pakistan's constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency, and Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months.

Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed.The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province.
The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants.

He was addressing a joint news conference in Islamabad this evening along with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister for Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry, and MNA Samar Bilour.

Azam Nazeer Tarar said under the Constitution, the provincial government led by the Chief Minister has ceased to exist. He said all the powers that rested with the Chief Minister, the provincial cabinet, and the advisors have been handed over to the Governor.

He further said that under another proclamation, a separate Secretariat has been established under the Governor and the Chief Secretary to run affairs of twelve districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa which will be directly under the Federation.

source_propositions.source_text: A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocked Panama on Friday, collapsing buildings and roads in the center of the country and injuring at least 27 people, with no deaths reported.
The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System.
The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia told AFP that there were no reports of fatalities so far.
In Panama City, about 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers.
"I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks.
"Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking."
A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall.

Benjamin Gonzalez, 52, said he was at a farm near the town of La Miel when the quake hit, and when he returned home he found "many houses devastated" and "everyone terrified" in the small town square, which was left without power.

items.sourceTitle: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'

source_propositions.source_text: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function.
Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty".

Five more deaths reported on Thursday, taking this year's toll to 294 -- already well above the 220 deaths recorded during the corresponding period last year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) on Thursday reported 1,935 new hospitalisations due to the mosquito-borne viral disease, taking the total caseload to 94,151.
Of the total hospitalisations, 88,208 patients have been discharged from hospitals after recovery.
The number of cases has already doubled compared with the corresponding period in 2025.
The DGHS registered 52,104 cases during the corresponding period last year.
October has so far recorded 49 deaths, compared with 114 in September.

"We don't have a plan right now to facilitate private hospitals with government funds to dedicate beds for patients who cannot afford private care. However, we have suggested that private hospitals consider the financial condition of dengue patients," the DGHS director added.

"The real situation may be up to 10 times higher than the reported cases. We don't have the exact data; we only report partial cases based on data provided by hospitals. The death rate in Bangladesh is the highest in the world. To take proper action and precautionary measures, exact data is crucial," he explained.
The country reported its highest-ever annual number of dengue deaths in 2022, when 281 people died.
Bangladesh usually sees a dengue season between June and September.

source_propositions.source_text: A key piece of the Carney government's economic agenda, Bill C-39, passed its first vote in the House of Commons on Thursday, with Conservatives and the majority Liberals sending the bill for study by a special committee.
The 243-page bill proposes to extend the government's approach to major infrastructure projects to other projects across the country.
The government wants those projects to undergo one review instead of several reviews, and to have that single review completed within one year.
The legislation is a core part of the Liberals' plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets.

Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to committee in order to propose amendments to what he called a "weak, watered-down, long-delayed" bill.
Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers' rights.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says his party will be proposing amendments to Bill C-39.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will use a special committee formed to study the sweeping legislation.
Carney government to study new major projects bill with tool last used in Harper era Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said she also asked for committee standing but was denied.

Critics warn Bill C-39 puts environment at risk At a news conference Thursday with labour and First Nations leaders, Davies and NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the legislation must not pass as written because of what it does to labour and treaty rights.
Also on Thursday, Cold Lake First Nations filed in Federal Court for a judicial review of Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project in the national interest.
The First Nation accuses the government of failing to adequately consult with them on the project.

source_propositions.source_text: Ontario to begin removing Toronto bike lanes.
Here's what you need to know Ontario will begin removing bike lanes from a stretch on Bloor Street W. in Etobicoke on Tuesday, the Ministry of Transportation says.
A notice of construction start, issued by the ministry, says the work will occur on a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road.
Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, confirmed in an email on Thursday that bike lane removal will begin Oct.

"Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday," Brasier said.
T he Court of Appeal ruled in August that Premier Doug Ford’s government could rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said Thursday that the removal of the bike lanes is "completely unacceptable" and an affront to the city by Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

"That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city. Whether it is bike lanes, speed cameras, Island airport, every element we need to have our say. The city belong to all of us Torontonians through the municipal government," she said.

The ministry-issued notice says existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs will be removed and new pavement markings and signs "to safely restore" an additional vehicle lane in each direction will be installed.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says of the bike lane removal: 'That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city.'

Michael Longfield, executive director of local cycling advocacy group CycleTO, said the organization is "outraged but not surprised" that the government has rejected the mayor's "win-win offer" to restore car lanes but keep bike lanes in Etobicoke.

"Ripping out these protected bike lanes against the will of Toronto city council is a colossal waste of $48 million. The province’s own experts know it will not ease traffic congestion, it will put people’s lives at risk, and there is no network of side streets that could replace these lanes."

sources.title: China proposes new labor protections for gig workers
propositions: 8 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Thursday released draft measures aimed at safeguarding the rights and interests of workers in new forms of employment, inviting public feedback until Nov.

If adopted, these measures would bring into the protection of the labor legal system those workers in new forms of employment who are subject to labor management by enterprises but whose arrangements do not fully meet the criteria for establishing a labor relationship.
It would be the first time China has done so through departmental rules.

The draft sets out provisions for protecting basic labor rights and interests, regulates labor rules and algorithms, and establishes rules for different forms of employment arrangements used by enterprises.
It also seeks to facilitate the resolution of labor disputes and clarify the regulatory responsibilities of government departments and legal liabilities for violations of the measures.
Members of the public can submit comments online via the ministry's website, by post or via email.

source_propositions.source_text: On October 7, 2026, the U.S.

Department of the Treasury (“Treasury”) announced its first enforcement action under the Outbound Investment Security Program (“OISP”), imposing a $200,000 civil penalty on Amidi, LLC (“Amidi”), a U.S. investor, for failing to submit a required notification for an investment by its controlled Chinese subsidiary in a Chinese artificial intelligence company.

The penalty is notable not only because it is the first, but also because it suggests Treasury is prepared to bring enforcement actions that target investments undertaken by U.S. persons’ controlled foreign entities, even where the investments are relatively small and arguably may not implicate the core policy concerns that motivated the OISP.

The importance of these early enforcement signals goes beyond compliance with the current OISP: they will carry increased importance in light of Treasury’s forthcoming regulations to strengthen and update the OISP under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (“COINS”) Act of 2025, especially given the National Security Science and Technology Strategy’s recent indication that the “Trump Administration will expand Outbound to encompass additional restrictions on U.S. investments in other areas implicated by China’s military-civil fusion strategy.”

According to Treasury, on April 19, 2025, a Chinese investment fund controlled by Amidi invested approximately $92,478 in Shanghai Qiongche Intelligent Technology Company Limited (“Noematrix”), a private Chinese company that develops artificial intelligence systems for robotics applications.

Treasury concluded that the investment was subject to the OISP’s notification requirements and imposed a $200,000 civil penalty after determining that Amidi did not submit the required post-closing notification.
Treasury’s announcement emphasizes that the violation involved a transaction undertaken by a controlled foreign entity of a U.S. person.

allowed_exact_dates.basis: October 11, 2026

source_propositions.source_text: The first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was achieved on October 11, 2026, marking a major milestone in Bangladesh's first nuclear power project as the reactor entered its initial criticality stage ahead of electricity generation.
The chain reaction marks the first of four stages before the plant can generate electricity.
The subsequent stages involve thermal energy transfer, mechanical energy conversion, and finally electricity generation and supply to the national grid.

Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, confirmed the development to The Business Standard, saying the reaction was initiated after the required compliance procedures, technical parameters and external certifications had been completed.
"On October 11, 2026 at 3:34pm, we were able to achieve the chain reaction smoothly. By the grace of Allah, the parameters were within the desired ranges, and the reactor was very stable," he said.
Inside a nuclear reactor, a controlled chain reaction splits uranium atoms through nuclear fission, releasing energy as heat.
That heat is used to generate steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity.

sources.title: The climate crisis is robbing Bangladesh’s girls of their futures
propositions: I often reflect on Nelson Mandela's words: "There can be no keener revelation of a society's soul than the way in which it treats its children."
Perhaps there is no better test of this than how a society treats its girls.
During a recent visit to Satkhira in southwestern Bangladesh, I met Tania, a 17-year-old who wants to return to school.
Tania's school was four kilometres from her home, a walk she took every day.
In monsoon, flooded roads and thick mud made it nearly impossible to go to school regularly.
She and her sister stayed at home most of the time.

source_propositions.source_text: <p>While other students were preparing to enrol in college after completing secondary school, Tania of Satkhira was struggling to stop her own marriage.
Meanwhile, the results of the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examination were published.

Astonishing everyone, she achieved not only a GPA of 5 but also A+ grades in every subject. She scored 100 out of 100 in chemistry and 99 in physics.</p><p>Yet she felt no joy at her remarkable achievement. Her mind was consumed by anxiety over her impending marriage and uncertainty about her future.

Ultimately, thanks to the support of her teachers and her outstanding SSC results, the determined Tania managed to escape child marriage this time.</p><p>Today, Sunday, is the International Day of the Girl Child.
This year’s theme is “End Child Marriage, Invest in Girls’ Rights”.

Nevertheless, among women aged 20–24, 47.2 per cent were married before turning 18, while 13.4 per cent were married before the age of 15.</p><p>The survey also found that the proportion of married women aged 15–19 rose from 32.9 per cent in 2019 to 38.9 per cent over the seven-year period.

But the story took a turn when Tania and her mother visited Akleema Khatun, the school’s information and communication technology teacher, with sweets to celebrate Tania’s excellent results.</p><p>Tania recalled that the teacher told her mother, “She has achieved such good results. How can you marry her off like this? We have taught your daughter for five years. We also have a claim on her future.”</p>.<p>The teacher, along with fellow teacher Foyezul Haque and local human rights activist Sakibur Rahman, then began trying to persuade Tania’s family to abandon the marriage plan.</p><p>Eventually, they took Tania to the upazila nirbahi officer (UNO), or upazila executive officer.

An educated mother, he said, can provide the greatest courage in such adverse circumstances.</p><p>Tania has enrolled in the first year of higher secondary education in the science stream at Satkhira Government College.

A 2025 survey found that only 59.2 per cent of children under five had been registered at birth.</p><p>Under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, the minimum legal age for marriage is 18 for women and 21 for men.

items.sourceTitle: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft

source_propositions.source_text: Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not.
Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted.
The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts.

For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal.
Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place.

“Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842.
Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply.
India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver.
That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years.

“I don’t know what our future looks like anymore. Sometimes I think about what will happen to this craft and I cry. This wasn’t just our profession; it was our identity, our heritage and everything we were known for.”

source_propositions.source_text: A Mi'kmaw community in Cape Breton is placing a big bet on new technology that it says can turn seawater into environmentally friendly jet fuel.

Eskasoni First Nation has invested $1.5 million and is the majority owner in a joint venture called eFuels Mi'kmaq Limited that plans to build a pilot project on band-owned land in Cape Breton Regional Municipality's industrial park in Sydney harbour.

Bertram Bernard, a band councillor and chair of Eskasoni Corporate Services, said the investment will create local jobs for band members and is an important step in taking a meaningful role in a growing industry.

"For us, this is about creating long-term economic opportunities, while continuing to be responsible stewards of our land and waters," he said during an announcement Thursday at the Sarah Denny Cultural Centre in Eskasoni.

The newly formed eFuels Mi'kmaq plans to extract hydrogen from seawater and draw carbon dioxide from the air to create what is known as drop-in fuel, meaning it can be burned like any other fuel without any engine modifications.
The process is expected to be powered by wind energy from onshore and offshore sources as they become available.
Eskasoni band councillor Bertram Bernard says the joint venture will create lasting economic benefits while ensuring stewardship of resources.

sources.title: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal
propositions: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.

“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.
China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers.
Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery.

sources.title: EU and China clinch deal to curb hybrid car exports
propositions: Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič says the agreement could prevent millions of Chinese vehicles from entering the European market over the next four years.
The European Union and China reached an agreement on Friday that will curb China’s booming hybrid car exports, delivering a breakthrough in negotiations aimed at rebalancing their trade relationship.

The announcement came as Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič wrapped up two days of talks in Beijing, the culmination of a push launched in June to narrow the bloc’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China.
The deal marks a win for the EU executive, which has been under pressure to secure concessions from Beijing.
Going into the talks, France and Germany strengthened Šefčovič’s hand by calling for the EU to take tough action on trade if China failed to curb a growing export glut.
Speaking in Beijing, the commissioner said the two sides had reached an agreement that would help to shield European automakers from low-price Chinese competition.

source_propositions.source_text: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said.

Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains.
The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation.
The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU. He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.”
The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year.
China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures.

Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value.

The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics.
“As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement.
“The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.”

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.

“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.
China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers.
Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery.
Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič says the agreement could prevent millions of Chinese vehicles from entering the European market over the next four years.
The European Union and China reached an agreement on Friday that will curb China’s booming hybrid car exports, delivering a breakthrough in negotiations aimed at rebalancing their trade relationship.

The announcement came as Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič wrapped up two days of talks in Beijing, the culmination of a push launched in June to narrow the bloc’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China.
The deal marks a win for the EU executive, which has been under pressure to secure concessions from Beijing.
Going into the talks, France and Germany strengthened Šefčovič’s hand by calling for the EU to take tough action on trade if China failed to curb a growing export glut.
Speaking in Beijing, the commissioner said the two sides had reached an agreement that would help to shield European automakers from low-price Chinese competition.

source_propositions.source_text: TAU researchers discover a new insect species from the age of the dinosaurs, revealing an unusual feeding mechanism that has disappeared from the insect world today. • Tel Aviv University researchers identified a previously unknown insect species preserved in 99-million-year-old amber from the age of the dinosaurs. • The new species, Cretodorus noonoo, nicknamed “Noo-Noo,” had exceptionally long, flexible mouthparts reaching nearly twice its body length. • Researchers believe these mouthparts helped the insect reach sugar-rich fluids deep inside cracks in tree bark. • The discovery reveals an ancient evolutionary adaptation with almost no modern equivalent and offers new insights into the ecosystems of Cretaceous forests.
Some 99 million years ago, during the age of the dinosaurs, a tiny insect belonging to a species previously unknown to science became trapped in tree resin.

The resin hardened and turned into amber, and the fossil preserved within it has now enabled a team of researchers from the School of Zoology and The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History to identify and describea new species: Cretodorus noonoo, or “Noo-Noo.”

Alongside the description of the new species, the study reveals an extraordinary biological adaptation that characterized Noo-Noo and its close relatives: exceptionally long and flexible mouthparts, which in Noo-Noo reached nearly twice the length of its body.

The researchers believe that this unusual structure enabled the insects to reach food sources that were inaccessible to insects with more rigid mouthparts, deep inside cracks and crevices in tree bark.

The study, published in the journal Insects, was conducted by Dolev Fabrikant and Dr Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of the School of Zoology, Wise Faculty of Life Sciences, The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History and New Environmental School at Tel Aviv University, in collaboration with Dr Yanzhe Fu of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The newly described species - Cretoduros noonoo, Photo credit: Dolev Fabrikant The researchers examined insect fossils belonging to Neazoniidae, an ancient family of planthoppers, including 13 specimens preserved in Kachin amber from Myanmar.
The ancient insects examined in the study, however, were found to possess extremely elongated mouthparts, the surface of which was densely covered with transverse folds.

items.sourceTitle: New large docodont fossil sheds light on Jurassic mammaliaform diversity

source_propositions.source_text: 11 (Xinhua) -- An international team led by Chinese scientists has discovered a new docodont mammaliaform species, the largest known of its kind, in Jurassic strata dating back about 160 million years, enriching scientific understanding of Jurassic mammaliaform diversity.

The new species has been named Megacauda sungei. Its fossil specimen, discovered in Ningcheng, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, measures roughly 52 centimeters in length and is estimated to have weighed around 2 kilograms, making it the largest known docodont mammaliaform. Its skull is clearly preserved, its trunk is robust, and its most striking feature is an unusually long, coiled tail.
The specimen also retains well-preserved pelvic bones, hind limbs and tail vertebrae, suggesting it was adapted for swimming.
Based on its distinctive teeth, researchers believe it could have hunted small animals living in the same environment, with a lifestyle possibly similar to that of the modern platypus.
The study also sheds light on the animal's throat structure.
The study was published online in the journal Nature on Oct.

"Mammaliaforms from the Mesozoic are often imagined as tiny creatures under dinosaur feet, but Megacauda sungei clearly raises the size limit of this group," said Li Yikun, an associate professor at Shenyang Normal University in northeast China.

The clang of hammers and crowbars echoed across Alam-Khankandi village yesterday morning as families dismantled their own homes, racing against a river that has already devoured four char villages and is eating into a fifth.
In two years, 1,803 families in five villages have lost their homes to erosion of char land beside the Padma Bridge.
Of them, 303 families in Alam-Khankandi have been displaced since August, according to the Shariatpur Water Development Board (WDB) and Purba Naodoba Union Parishad.
About 150 families still living in the village are at imminent risk.
The char emerged about three decades ago in Painpara mouza on the northern bank of the Padma.
According to WDB sources, the char formed Naodoba Union Parishad, which includes six villages and constitutes wards 2 and 3.
During a visit yesterday, this correspondent found families preparing to leave.
“Five days ago, nine bighas of cultivated land were lost in river erosion. Now where will my daughter go with her four children?”
For Md Shahid Fakir, 38, erosion destroyed both his livelihood and his house.
“Having lost everything to river erosion, I am now destitute. I have no place to call my own anymore,” he said.

source_propositions.source_text: HANAPEPE (HawaiiNewsNow) - The 22 Kauai families keeping traditional Hawaiian salt making alive in Hanapepe are seeking the community’s help to restore their harvest site.
Storm surge from Hurricane Lowell drastically changed the area.
“The sand dunes were depleted. It was gone. It was a new landscape. I didn’t recognize it,” said Malia Nobrega-Olivera.
Nobrega-Olivera and her ‘ohana have been Hawaiian salt makers for decades. She said the storm damage was the worst she’s seen.
“It is different from all of my 55 years growing up in Hanapepe. It was a new space,” she said.
Lowell pushed incredible amounts of sand into the beach park and salt beds, changing the composition of the land, making the clay more porous.
Together, they’re hosting a community work day on Saturday to restore the area.
There have been floods in recent years, and the group was already working on a dune restoration project.
But if conditions aren’t right, that number is drastically less.
The workday runs from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., and more will be scheduled in the future.
To stay connected with the group, contact them online at ProtectPaakai.org .

sources.title: Webb Measures Distance to Farthest Fast Radio Burst, Suggesting Origin - NASA Science
propositions: First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe.
Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again.
Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date.
Their finding has implications for what kind of energetic event creates these bursts.

“What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them. We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof,” said Manisha Caleb of the University of Sydney, lead author on the study published Thursday in the journal Science.
The MeerTRAP team used the MeerKAT telescope to detect the burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.

sources.title: South Africa’s MeerKAT combines with NASA’s Webb to pinpoint the most distant cosmic Fast Radio Burst - South African Radio Astronomy Observatory - NRF-SARAO
propositions: Record breaker dates back to just 3 billion years after the big bang.

Astronomers using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have discovered and precisely localized the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves lasting only a few milliseconds that travelled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.
FRBs are enigmatic objects whose brief radio flashes are detectable half-way across the universe.
First identified in 2007, their origins remain uncertain, particularly since most are seen only once.
The research reported today started with the discovery by the MeerTRAP team of a radio burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.
The MeerKAT data precisely localized the FRB and suggested that it was extremely distant, but to measure the distance accurately astronomers would need to study its host galaxy.

source_propositions.source_text: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds.
In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age.
Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered.
Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified.

Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time.
The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times.
We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth.

These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy.

The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found.

Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies.
Lead image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Themiya Nanayakkara (USYD), Joseph DePasquale (STScI), CC BY Manisha Caleb is a senior lecturer in astrophysics at the University of Sydney.

First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe. Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again.

Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date. Their finding has implications for what kind of energetic event creates these bursts.

“What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them. We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof,” said Manisha Caleb of the University of Sydney, lead author on the study published Thursday in the journal Science.
The MeerTRAP team used the MeerKAT telescope to detect the burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.
Record breaker dates back to just 3 billion years after the big bang.

Astronomers using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have discovered and precisely localized the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves lasting only a few milliseconds that travelled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.
FRBs are enigmatic objects whose brief radio flashes are detectable half-way across the universe.
First identified in 2007, their origins remain uncertain, particularly since most are seen only once.
The research reported today started with the discovery by the MeerTRAP team of a radio burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.
The MeerKAT data precisely localized the FRB and suggested that it was extremely distant, but to measure the distance accurately astronomers would need to study its host galaxy.

items.sourceTitle: FoN Campaign Defends Ghana's Expanded Fishing Zone

sources.title: FoN declares zero tolerance for mining in the ocean | Ghana News Agency
propositions: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Dixcove (W/R), Oct.

08, GNA – Friends of the Nation (FoN), a non-government organisation (NGO), has declared zero tolerance for mining activities in the ocean as part of its efforts to ensure justice in fisheries governance.

The declaration followed government’s proposed offshore gold reconnaissance deal, granting 10 contiguous offshore reconnaissance licences to Gold Coast Resources Ghana Limited to undertake gold mining in Ghana’s marine waters from Half-Assini in Jomoro to Winneba in the Effutu Municipality in the Western and Central Regions.
According to the NGO, gold mining in the high seas would disrupt the activities of artisanal fishers, thereby bringing fishing expeditions to a standstill.
Mr Mevuta Donkris, the Executive Director of the FoN, said this at a day’s workshop for stakeholders in the fishing industry at Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region.

It was organised by FoN under the project dubbed “Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future” and was attended by chief fishermen and women from Lower and Upper Dixcove, canoe owners, fish mongers, fishers, the Fisheries Commission, FoN and the media.

source_propositions.source_text: Government has doubled Ghana's Inshore Exclusive Zone from six to 12 nautical miles for artisanal fishers — now Friends of the Nation is training coastal communities in Ahanta West to stop trawlers from crossing the new line.

Barely days after a canoe fisherman in Butre spoke of his fears that marine protection rules could push small-scale operators further out to sea, an environmental NGO has launched a campaign aimed at making sure the opposite happens — that industrial trawlers, not artisanal canoes, are kept out of protected waters.

Friends of the Nation (FoN) launched its "Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future" campaign at a day-long workshop held in Upper and Lower Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region on 11 October 2026, according to the Ghana News Agency (GNA).
The workshop brought together fishers, fishmongers and other industry stakeholders to explain recent regulatory changes and the boundaries of Ghana's newly expanded Inshore Exclusive Zone (IEZ).
The IEZ is a stretch of sea reserved exclusively for canoe fishers and other small-scale, artisanal operators, where larger industrial vessels are barred from casting nets.
According to FoN, government has extended this protected zone from six nautical miles to 12 nautical miles offshore, effectively doubling the area set aside for Ghana's coastal fishing communities.
Mevuta Donkris, FoN's Executive Director, thanked government for the extension but cautioned that the new boundary would only mean something if fishers themselves remained alert, GNA reports.

A security researcher says data presented at a regional meeting in Senegal shows about 2,000 illegal migrants entered Ghana between March 2025 and July 2026, renewing calls for stronger border controls.

items.sourceTitle: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender.

source_propositions.source_text: Koch, at 103, has been perfecting his one-liners for decades. He deals them out quickly, with a half smile that reveals the four remaining teeth on his top gums and a flash of mischief in his clear blue eyes.
After 63 years tending bar, he has his setup-pause-punch line down to a science.
When a patron on a recent evening asks him whether he is the oldest bartender in the world, he doesn’t miss a beat.
“Don’t ask me,” he says.
“I haven’t been around the world yet.”
By many unofficial accounts, Irv (as he is widely known) is indeed the world’s oldest bartender.
The first of them, decades ago, was named Amy.
“When the first one gets here, that’s when it opens up.”
And after Irv’s wife and brother died, “he never stopped,” Cook says.
Right now, he’s excited for his 104th birthday party in August.
“But everybody should come on down and check us out while they still can. And meet the famous Irv.”
